content: A Biomedical Equipment Technician (BMET) plays a critical role in the healthcare delivery system. These highly skilled professionals are employed by hospitals, clinics, and the military to ensure that medical equipment is functional, safe, and properly configured to meet the operational needs of healthcare organizations. Their responsibilities include the installation, inspection, repair, calibration, preventive maintenance, education, and modification of biomedical equipment and support systems. BMETs provide guidance to medical staff and other agencies on the operational theory, basic physiological principles, and safe clinical application of biomedical equipment. This ensures that patient care and medical staff equipment are maintained to the highest standards. The profession gained significant recognition in 1970 when consumer advocate Ralph Nader highlighted the dangers of electrical accidents in hospitals, emphasizing the need for skilled technicians to mitigate such risks. BMETs work across a wide range of fields and devices within the biomedical and clinical engineering domain. Examples of the technologies they manage include radiographic and fluoroscopic X-ray systems, diagnostic ultrasound, lasers, mammography, telemedicine, film image processing, nuclear medicine, gamma cameras, positron emission tomography (PET), medical imaging, computed tomography (CT), electron microscopes, picture archiving and communication systems (PACS), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanners, physiological monitoring systems, sterilization equipment, dental and optometry devices, surgical and anesthesia systems, laboratory equipment, dialysis machines, respiratory services (e.g., ventilators), computers, and information technology systems. BMETs collaborate closely with medical supply personnel to procure parts, supplies, and equipment. They also work with facility management teams to coordinate equipment installations that may require specific facility modifications. Regulatory Issues BMETs must adhere to federal and state safety regulations. Most biomedical systems require documentation to demonstrate that they have been managed, modified, tested, delivered, and used according to a planned and approved quality assurance process. This approach enhances the safety and quality of diagnostic and therapeutic equipment by employing risk management practices to minimize the likelihood of harm to patients or staff. In the United States, BMETs operate under various regulatory frameworks. Clinical devices and technologies are typically governed by agencies and standards such as the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), National Fire Protection Agency (NFPA 99 and NFPA 70), Life Safety Code 101, Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 21, Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), and the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations (JCAHO). Compliance with these codes and standards is essential for the U.S. government registry of biomedical devices. Other countries have their own regulatory mechanisms. Biomedical Equipment Technology Training Traditionally, biomedical equipment technology is an interdisciplinary field pursued after completing an associate degree in Biomedical Equipment Technology, Biomedical Electronics Technology, or Biomedical Engineering Technology. Some BMETs receive their training through military programs. Entry-level BMETs typically hold a two-year associate degree or complete approximately one year of full-time military training. A four-year graduate in this field is considered an applied engineer and may perform similar duties to clinical engineers, BMET managers, or directors/executives. Practical experience is often gained through internships, and continuing education is provided by medical device manufacturers through service schools. Professional Certification Many BMETs pursue professional certifications, such as becoming a Certified Biomedical Equipment Technician (CBET) by meeting specific educational requirements and passing an examination. Additional certifications include Certified Radiology Equipment Specialists (CRES) and Certified Laboratory Equipment Specialists (CLES). While the CBET title is not mandatory, it is highly respected within the technical community. Employment BMETs may work in a hospital's Biomedical or Clinical Engineering Department, for third-party independent service organizations (ISOs), or for original equipment manufacturers (OEMs). Those employed by OEMs or ISOs are often referred to as Field Service Engineers (FSEs). FSEs are specialized technicians who support service and sales operations. Both BMETs and FSEs face increased risks of exposure to electrical, mechanical, high-pressure steam, noise, bloodborne pathogens, lasers, chemicals, and nuclear contaminants. Military Roles Military BMETs receive comprehensive technical training down to the component level at the Department of Defense Biomedical Equipment Technician Training School. In addition to their military training, they may complete additional credits through institutions like Aims Community College to earn a degree with an emphasis on Biomedical Electronics Technology. In the U.S. Air Force, BMETs operate under job code 4A2X1, with skill levels represented by 3, 5, 7, or 9. The Air Force Instruction 41-201, Managing Clinical Engineering Programs, serves as a foundational guide for Air Force BMETs. In the U.S. Army, the Military Occupational Specialty (MOS) for BMETs is 68A, which was previously designated as 91A. Navy BMETs follow guidelines outlined in NAVMED P-5132. Contributions and Responsibilities BMETs manage a wide range of equipment and systems, requiring extensive communication with management and other healthcare disciplines. They are often called upon to make life-critical decisions in emergencies, working as part of a team to improve medical care delivery and cost-effectiveness. BMETs contribute to advancing processes and improving equipment and devices on a national scale. They are frequently relied upon as in-house experts for a broad range of challenges, monitoring safety throughout healthcare facilities, documenting trends, and coordinating service when direct repairs are not possible. Additionally, BMETs assist in selecting and creating new systems for hospitals both locally and globally.
